content.thinking:
I'm piecing together the timeline: the flag was fully off before 16:30, then at 16:30 saw a mixed rollout (134 off, 66 on), and by 16:31 it flipped to 100% on. That lines up exactly with the ZeroDivisionError appearing in spend_summary.py starting at 16:30, suggesting the monthly-spend-feature rollout triggered the crash.

Interestingly, there's no recorded production change event or flag-provider history entry for this shift besides Argus, even though the evaluation logs clearly show the flip happened — so the change itself seems to be missing from the official record. I'm now building the causal chain: account page requests started failing with errors, traced to the ZeroDivisionError, which in turn traces back to the flag beginning to evaluate "on" for a growing share of traffic.

The provider's own history shows no change by anyone but Argus, so the flag flip appears only in the log lines, not in the official change record. For ruled-out causes, I can cite no deployment recorded the day before onset (T9) and all replicas running a single revision at T10.1 (T10), though I can't rule out an earlier revision change since its deploy timing relative to onset isn't known — the rule is that it's ruled out only by measured health with it in place, not by elapsed time.

Checking the metrics: error rate held steady around 1% from 16:00 and account pages rendered normally between 16:20–16:25, consistent with baseline. Since no deploys happened in the prior day and the service measured healthy with that revision in place beforehand, the running revision itself is ruled out as the cause.

The flag history is more telling — provider records show no flag changes by any user, yet logs confirm the flag flipped, meaning the change wasn't reflected in provider history, only Argus's. Tracing the actual break: with the flag enabled, the spend summary divides this month's total spend by this month's purchase count, which is zero for returning shoppers who haven't bought yet this month, causing a ZeroDivisionError that matches the logged error.

There's no S or D row backing the reasoning behind this mechanism — it rests entirely on an unrun reading, F1, meaning the root cause does get reached but it's not fully verified. The rollout pattern in the logs also roughly lines up, with only a subset of evaluations flipped on before the full rollout.

I'm framing the cause in plain words: a setting enabling a monthly-spending feature started applying to shoppers, and its code likely divided by zero for anyone who'd bought before but not yet this month — the division by zero itself is confirmed by the log, but the "bought before, not this month" explanation is inferred from F1 rather than directly shown, and nothing in the record indicates who actually turned the setting on.

For contributing factors, I'm noting that the flag change never showed up in the flag provider's history or production change events — only in log lines — so Argus couldn't connect the onset to a recorded change and act on it. If the change had been properly recorded, Argus could have reverted the flag and shortened the incident, which points to an actionable fix: ensure every change to the monthly-spend feature flag gets logged in the flag provider.

I also want to flag investigating how the flag evaluation changed with no corresponding recorded change, since that gap is itself worth tracing down. Separately, there's a second factor: no test verified the spend summary behavior with the flag on for a shopper with zero purchases before the flag went live, which would have caught the division-by-zero error — suggesting a pre-launch check should be added for that case.

Looking at G971b, the flag went from partial rollout to fully on from 16:31 onward while errors were climbing, with no guard halting that progression — though I'm not fully sure if this was a staged rollout or a sudden flip, so I should phrase the finding carefully rather than assume. Either way, the fix should involve gating flag rollouts on rising error rates with automatic rollback.

For CF-4, nobody got paged for the HighErrorRate alert on io-shop, meaning no human had the chance to disable the flag manually — the fix is linking that alert to on-call paging, which is a legitimate factor that existed before the incident.

For the remaining items, I'm pulling together the detect/process steps: logging every flag change against the provider's history so it ties to an onset (CF-1), investigating how monthly-spend-feature got enabled without a recorded change (also CF-1), and turning the flag off as a mitigation until the real fix ships — though that last one seems more like something the record already flags as left to a person rather than a new corrective action.

Then for prevention, I need testing the flag-gated code path with shoppers who have no purchases before going live (CF-2), and building automatic halt-and-revert for flag rollouts when error rates spike (CF-3).

For lessons learned, I'm noting what went well: the investigator agent correctly placed the onset and built a causal link between the flag and the ZeroDivisionError, Argus appropriately declined to act since the change wasn't in the record, and the code-fix agent drafted PR #412 — though I should avoid describing what that fix actually does and make sure timed items start with who performed them. Nothing stands out yet for what went wrong.

That nobody was paged feels like its own finding — I'm debating whether to log it as a contributing factor (CF-4) or under went_wrong, along with the mismatch between the flag provider's history and the service logs showing the actual flip (CF-1), and whether escalation happened while the flag stayed on with no one paged to act.

I don't see a clear got_lucky item — the pre-existing ClientDisconnected errors and unaffected shoppers this month both feel like fault rather than luck, so I'll leave it empty.

For assumptions, I'm noting the flag flip is inferred from log evaluation counts rather than a recorded change, and the pre-onset ClientDisconnected errors are being treated as baseline.

For step 3, I'm drafting the phrasing around the monthly-spend-feature flag's evaluation counts shifting from all-off to partially-on then all-on, citing the specific log lines, and noting the flag provider's history shows no recorded change by anyone except Argus — meaning the switch is only visible through these log entries.

Now I need to reconsider ordering: the symptom is the ZeroDivisionError, but the chain should explain why that code ran (flag turned on) before explaining the mechanism (dividing by this month's purchase count, which is zero for many shoppers). I'm reworking the sequence so symptom leads to the error, then to why the flag enabled the code path, then to the zero-division mechanism itself.

I should keep step 1 figure-free, and I can cite G5309 if useful though it's not essential. For ruling out a deploy as the cause, I need to note that no release occurred the day before onset and all replicas stayed on one revision, with health checks confirming that revision was healthy.

I want to cite T9, T10, and Gad41 as evidence that the same revision was running when pages rendered normally and when the incident occurred, since no deploy was recorded. I also need to watch my wording — avoid number words like "one" and instead say "the same revision" to keep the prose figure-free.

I'm also realizing the zero-division issue needs careful phrasing: instead of saying "divides by zero," I should describe it as the calculation failing for shoppers who bought before but not this month, since dividing by an empty count causes the error. I'll keep timestamps as placeholders rather than writing them out directly.

action_items.item: Turn monthly-spend-feature off for io-shop until the proposed fix is merged and released.
Find out how monthly-spend-feature came to evaluate on for io-shop while the flag provider's history showed no change by anyone but Argus.
Make every flag change on io-shop, whoever or whatever makes it, show up in the flag provider's history and the production change events.
Before a flag is turned on in production, run the code it gates with the flag on in tests, including account page fixtures for shoppers with no purchases this month.
Make flag rollouts on io-shop halt and revert automatically when the service's error rate rises above its baseline.
Link the HighErrorRate alert on io-shop to an on-call rotation so that it pages a person.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers' account page requests failed, and the service's share of failed requests rose far above its usual level.
The failing account page requests raised ZeroDivisionError at src/io_shop/spend_summary.py:47. This error was not seen in the logs before the onset.

ruled_out.what: A deploy, release or new revision: no production change was read back for the day before the onset. At {T10.1} all replicas ran the same revision, and account pages rendered normally on it with the flag off before the onset.

causal_chain.step: The monthly-spend-feature flag began evaluating on. Before the onset every evaluation came back off (G7e5d). At {G971b.6}, {G971b.2} of {G971b.3} evaluations came back on (G971b), and from {Gce95.4} every evaluation was on (Gce95). This turned on the spend summary code that raises the error. The flag provider's history showed no flag change by anyone but Argus (T15), and the production change events showed none either (T9), so this switch shows up only in the service's own log lines.

With the flag on, average_spend_per_item_this_month divides the shopper's spend this month by their number of purchases this month. That count is empty for any shopper who has bought before but not this month, so the division fails.

input.cause_in_plain_words: The shop started serving a new monthly-spending feature on its account pages, and the feature's calculation divided by the number of purchases a shopper had made this month, which likely broke the page for anyone who had bought before but not yet this month.

contributing_factors.factor: The switch of monthly-spend-feature to on was not seen in the flag provider's history or in the production change events, only in the service's log lines. So the onset could not be tied to a recorded change, and Argus would not undo it.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: If the flag change had been recorded, Argus could have acted on C1 and turned the flag back off, which would have shortened the incident.
contributing_factors.label: CF-1

contributing_factors.factor: No check was seen that ran the spend summary with monthly-spend-feature on, for a shopper with no purchases this month, before the flag was turned on in production.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: The division failure would have been caught before the flag reached shoppers.
contributing_factors.label: CF-2

contributing_factors.factor: No guard was seen that halts or reverses a flag change when the error rate rises. The flag went from on for some evaluations to on for every evaluation while account page errors were already appearing.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: The flag would have stopped at some shoppers or been switched back off, which would have limited how many account pages failed and for how long.
contributing_factors.label: CF-3

contributing_factors.factor: HighErrorRate on io-shop paged nobody: no on-call incident was linked to it.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: A person would have known about it and could have turned the flag off, the step Argus left to a person, which would have shortened the incident.
contributing_factors.label: CF-4

went_well.item: The Investigator Agent formed C1, which pointed to the monthly-spend-feature flag turning on and to the ZeroDivisionError in the spend summary.
Argus declined to act on C1 because the change it names was not in the record of what changed, and left undoing it to a person.
The Code-Fix Agent proposed a fix as draft pull request #412.

input.root_cause: With monthly-spend-feature on, the account page's spend summary runs average_spend_per_item_this_month, which divides the shopper's spend this month by their number of purchases this month without handling an empty month. For a shopper who has bought before but not this month there is nothing to divide by, so the page raises ZeroDivisionError at spend_summary.py:47.
input.still_at_risk: While monthly-spend-feature stayed on, account pages could keep failing for any shopper who had bought before but not this month.
input.symptom: Shoppers' account pages failed to load
